submission.natural_language_explanation: This layer-0 pole is a lexical detector of the act of naming/designating: it fires on the current token when that token names, labels or confers a title or office — ' named' by far the strongest (~4.6 of 4.9), then name/names/naming, called/calls/calling, renamed/rename, designate(d)/designation, declared, termed, dubbed, christened, proclaimed, nominate(d)/nominating, appoint(ed), appellation, acronym, abbreviation, nickname/nicknamed, surname, refer(red), registry/registered, listed, and the election-to-office register elect/electing/elected/election(s), vote/voted/voting/voter, campaign, ballot, candidate, with the address formulas thank, wish and congratulate/congratulations clearing the line weakly (~1.3–1.9). It is exactly zero on the names and honorifics themselves (Carl, Raleigh, Charlotte, Mr, Dr, Sir, President, Saint, Mount), on ordinary verbs (walked, built, said, made, died), and on 'name' in other senses (namely, username, filename, game, same, title, label); activation is a pure function of the current token — identical across constructions, positions and topics — so a text is predicted active exactly when one of those designation tokens occurs in it.

Fifty-eight miles from the nearest hospital, the school at Cedar Hollow keeps its own generator, its own water tank and a pantry that has never run empty during a storm. The building dates from 1938, when the county consolidated four one-room schools into a single brick structure with tall windows and a coal furnace in the basement. For the first two decades, classes ran from September through May, and the older students spent their afternoons helping on the surrounding farms before returning for lessons in arithmetic and geography.

The furnace was replaced in 1974 by an oil burner, and the oil burner by a heat pump in 2009, after a grant from the state historic preservation office. The windows are original. Every spring a crew of volunteers reglazes the worst of them with putty and a hot iron, working from ladders that belong to the fire department in the next town.

The gym floor is maple, laid in 1952 and refinished so many times that the lines of the basketball court have drifted three inches from where they began. On winter evenings the whole valley seems to pass through the doors: the volunteer ambulance crew practises its drills there, the 4-H club meets in the cafeteria, and a quilting group works under the tall windows until the caretaker turns off the lights at ten.

Twice a year the parents hold a supper in the gym to raise money for the heating bill. The menu never changes: beans, cornbread, coleslaw and a table of pies baked by whoever volunteered that week. Last November the supper brought in enough to cover the fuel through February, which is the way it has worked for as long as anyone can remember.

She knows which families need a bag of groceries sent home on Friday and which children need a coat before the first cold snap. Snow closes the road over the ridge two or three times each winter, and the plough does not always come before the school day starts. Teachers have slept in the staff room rather than miss a morning, and the cook keeps a spare bag of flour in the pantry for exactly that reason.

Visitors often remark that the corridors smell of floor wax and chalk, and that the walls are hung with photographs of classes going back ninety years, row upon row of children squinting into the sun. The oldest photograph shows thirty-two students and a teacher standing on the front steps in the winter of 1939, the men in the back row already in uniform.
